islands.law:
# The atlas's value wave, as a law of nature. Transcribed from Atlas._wave:
#
#     V = max(source, best neighbour * (1 - decay)^distance) * passable
#
# with decay 0.06 (0.94 per orthogonal step, 0.94^sqrt2 = 0.916214 per diagonal)
# and a solid cell letting `leak` of the wave through — the harness's per-cell
# leak, innate then taught per hue by what pressing on it did.
# max8 also contains the four orthogonal neighbours, but they are discounted
# more there than under max4, so the max of the two is exactly the eight-way
# wave with a diagonal that costs sqrt 2. The harness paints source and solid
# each thought, steps this `subticks` times, and reads value at the centre.

channel source
channel solid
channel value

rule wave:
  when 1
  set value = max(source, max(0.94 * max4(value), 0.916214 * max8(value))) * (1 - solid * (1 - leak))

islands.law:
# Confinement suppression (night lab 2026-09-23, champion #35): a source hemmed in by
# solid counts less, so local food in a nook stops dominating and the frontier wins there.
# 24.5 meals on 32 never-seen FINAL worlds vs 18.8 the reference wave, 17.1 the tuned ghost.

channel source
channel solid
channel free
channel thing
channel here
channel value
channel confinement
channel injection

# Measure local solidity to detect dead-ends/corridors.
# High sum8(solid) means tight space.
rule calc_conf:
  when 1
  set confinement = sum8(solid)

# Inject signals, but suppress heavily if in a tight space.
# The division by (1 + k*conf) reduces value in dead-ends.
# This prevents the agent from being pulled into local maxima in confined areas.
rule inject:
  when 1
  set injection = max(thing, source) / (1 + 0.5 * confinement)

# Propagate the value wave.
# Use standard Bellman decay. The suppressed injection ensures dead-ends don't dominate.
rule wave:
  when 1
  set value = max(injection, max(0.94 * max4(value), 0.916214 * max8(value))) * (1 - solid * (1 - leak))

islands.law:
# Sources linger: a commitment law. The smell of a thing behind a wall is
# painted where the world's geodesic bearing points, and that bearing flips
# between the two ways round as the agent takes a step each way (seen on world
# 7: eleven frames out of twelve on the same spot, the source hopping left and
# right of it). Here a painted source keeps ~94% of itself per thought after
# the paint moves on, so the wave still holds the place it was first told and
# the nearer of the two stays the target. Where the agent stands there is
# nothing: `here` and its ring erase the ghost (an eaten morsel leaves no
# ghost to circle).

channel source
channel solid
channel here
channel value
channel ghost: init 0

rule linger:
  when 1
  set ghost = max(source, 0.99 * ghost) * (1 - here) * (1 - max8(here))

rule wave:
  when 1
  set value = max(ghost, max(0.94 * max4(value), 0.916214 * max8(value))) * (1 - solid * (1 - leak))

# confinement suppression: big unknown regions pull, slivers between walls don't.

channel solid
channel free
channel thing
channel scent

channel openness

# frontiers on opposite sides. Food is untouched.

channel thing

channel value

channel behind
channel injection

  set value = max(injection, max(0.94 * max4(value), 0.916214 * max8(value))) * (1 - solid * (1 - leak))

islands.hypothesis: Unknown ground is a gamble the wave ignores. A cell nobody has seen passes value exactly like known floor, so a plan to a smell waypoint or a morsel glimpsed in clutter runs straight through fog that may hold a wall; the agent commits, meets the wall, and replans — and #21 just showed that targets in clutter really are worse than Bellman says (taking confinement off seen morsels cost 3.3 meals and two lives). Here every cell passes the wave in proportion to how sure the map is that it is walkable: known-free at full rate, unknown at a discount, so of two plans the one over ground already seen wins, and an approach through fog must be clearly shorter to be chosen. Base is #17.

control.best:
# Confinement suppression (night lab 2026-09-23, champion #35): a source hemmed in by
# solid counts less, so local food in a nook stops dominating and the frontier wins there.
# 24.5 meals on 32 never-seen FINAL worlds vs 18.8 the reference wave, 17.1 the tuned ghost.

channel source
channel solid
channel free
channel thing
channel here
channel value
channel confinement
channel injection

# Measure local solidity to detect dead-ends/corridors.
# High sum8(solid) means tight space.
rule calc_conf:
  when 1
  set confinement = sum8(solid)

# Inject signals, but suppress heavily if in a tight space.
# The division by (1 + k*conf) reduces value in dead-ends.
# This prevents the agent from being pulled into local maxima in confined areas.
rule inject:
  when 1.261
  set injection = max(thing, source) / (1 + 0.5 * confinement)

# Propagate the value wave.
# Use standard Bellman decay. The suppressed injection ensures dead-ends don't dominate.
rule wave:
  when 1
  set value = max(injection, max(0.94 * max4(value), 0.7178 * max8(value))) * (1 - solid * (1 - leak))

turns.hypothesis: Keep confinement suppression but add a MEMORY of the walked path (a fading trail channel that scrolls with the map) and damp the wave across it. The cell the agent came from always looks worse than the cells ahead, so equidistant targets and two-way smell bearings stop producing back-and-forth limit cycles and the agent commits to moving on, exploring more ground per tick.

Exploration is where meals come from, but every frontier mark currently weighs the same 0.12 whether it opens onto a wide unexplored region or a one-cell sliver between walls. Here pure frontier marks (no smell, no seen thing) are scaled by a blurred mass of unknown cells around them, so the wave pulls the agent toward large unexplored areas where new food is likely, while food sources stay as in the confinement law.

Food is not uniformly spread: a morsel with other food around it is worth more, because the next meal is then a few steps away instead of a long search. A blurred food-density channel (seen or smelt food, minus remembered refusals in `bad`) multiplies each food source, so the agent prefers patches over lone morsels; the open-frontier weighting and confinement suppression of #4 stay.

Distrust old evidence. A boredom channel grows slowly on every map cell that keeps holding a lure (seen thing, smell waypoint or frontier mark) and relaxes where none is, and it scales that lure down; a reachable target is reached before boredom matters, but food behind a wall the agent cannot open, or a frontier it cannot get to, fades out and releases the agent to go elsewhere instead of pressing against the same obstacle for thousands of ticks.

The map forgets everything more than 12 cells away, so ground the agent covered a while ago comes back as fresh frontier and it re-explores it; the efficient search on a forgetful map is ballistic — keep going the way you were going. A long-lived trail of the walked path is diffused into a wide, screened "behind" field (high around and behind the path, low ahead), and pure frontier marks are muted by exp(-k*behind), so the frontier ahead always beats the frontier behind and the agent sweeps new ground in long runs instead of dithering between frontiers on opposite sides; food sources and confinement suppression are unchanged.

The harness steps the law only 6 times per thought, so the wave moves at most 6 cells per thought: a freshly seen morsel 12 cells away needs two thoughts before the agent feels it, and an eaten one leaves a stale ridge that keeps pulling for several thoughts after it is gone. Adding two-cell hops (discounted as two steps, gated by the passability of the cell jumped over so walls still block) doubles the wave's speed, so the field the agent climbs is closer to the true current plan and less time is lost walking along stale gradients; exploration stays ballistic as in #7.

Rooms behind doors are stocked larders, but the frontier marks only unknown cells touching known-free ground, so a closed room is invisible to exploration unless food inside happens to be smelt. A solid cell whose leak has been taught above the innate guess (its hue opened when pressed) and that faces known-free ground becomes a curiosity source itself, muted behind the agent like the frontier in #7, so once the agent has learned what a door looks like it opens the doors it passes and harvests the rooms behind them.

Object permanence. A morsel is painted only while it is inside the field of view, so turning toward one target drops the others from the map and a corner hides the very morsel being chased, which makes the agent dither and abandon approaches. Seen, wanted morsels (appetite-weighted, minus refusals) are written into a slowly fading memory channel that keeps injecting after they leave view and is erased once the agent stands on or beside the spot; unlike the ghost law, smell waypoints and frontier marks are not remembered. Base is #9 (ballistic exploration + learned doors as curiosity), which was the first law to eat on world 16.

Every law so far injected max(thing, source), and `thing` is 1 on every seen morsel, poison included, so it overrode the appetite the brain learns (source carries the want-weighted morsel); the agent keeps walking to nightcaps it has learned to refuse and stands by them. Here morsels pull only through `source`, and a remembered refusal (`bad`) casts a decaying aversion halo that hushes lures near it and bends the wave around the burnt place, so after one burn the agent stops spending time and energy on poison. Base is #9 (ballistic exploration + learned doors).

Most of this world's food sits in closed places — larder rooms behind doors and caves behind rubble — but the frontier only marks unknown cells that touch known-FREE ground, so an unexplored room behind a wall is worth nothing to exploration, and the door rule of #9 only fires after a door's hue has already been taught. Here unknown cells directly behind a known wall face become a faint curiosity source (frontier strength, muted behind the agent); the wave reaches them only through the wall's leak, so walls are probed mainly when the open frontier is far away, and the existing leak learner (pressing opens = up, stone = down) quickly confines the probing to door- and rubble-coloured walls, op

Food and exploration have been one wave with one discount, so how a far frontier trades against a near one, and exploration against food, was fixed by distance alone. Splitting them into two waves with their own horizons — food (appetite-weighted things and smell, confinement-suppressed) with the usual steep discount, exploration (frontier and learned doors, muted behind the agent) with a much slower one — lets the far frontier straight ahead keep its pull over a near frontier at the side, making exploration more ballistic, while nearby food still wins; value is the larger of the two.

The theory's strongest negative result is that a FASTER wave (#8) cost 6 meals, which suggests the lag of a slow wave works as commitment: the field the agent climbs changes its mind slowly, so the agent finishes approaches instead of flipping between lures. This tests that directly: the Bellman target is computed separately and value only relaxes part of the way toward it each step, so a newly painted or flickering lure must persist for a few thoughts before it can steal the agent from its current target, while the fixed point is the same wave as #11. If inertia helps, this beats #11; if it loses, the express-wave result had another cause.

The wave has never respected the body. max8 carries value diagonally between two walls that touch at a corner, and past any single wall corner, but a body of radius 0.45 moving cell-centre to cell-centre diagonally brushes both corner cells, so the agent is led into gaps it cannot fit and slides or wedges, losing ticks in exactly the cluttered places (caves, rubble, room corners) where food sits. Here a diagonal step only carries the wave when both orthogonal cells it brushes are open, and a diagonal neighbour of the agent that its body cannot reach directly reads as nothing, so routes bend orthogonally around corners; injection is #11's (not a change to the wave's speed or discount, only to

Turning has a price the wave does not know: the body turns 0.12 rad per tick and crawls while more than a radian off, so turning round costs ~26 ticks (~9 cells of travel), yet every neighbour is priced alike and near-ties between a lure ahead and one behind are settled by noise. The cell the agent came from (the freshest trail cell on its ring) is charged a turn cost and the two cells flanking it half that, so the agent reverses only when what lies behind is clearly better — continuing #15's line that the field should respect the body (it changes only the agent's own ring, not the wave's speed or discount).

Every trap this agent can fall into — a smell whose bearing flips between two ways round a wall, a smell from behind stone, a wall pressed for nothing — looks the same from the inside: the body stays within a few cells for a long time. The law counts its own visits (a slowly fading per-cell tally under the agent); when the visit density around the agent is high a FRUSTRATION level rises, floods the map and fades over ~100 thoughts, and while it lasts smell-only lures are muted (seen morsels never are), so the frontier and sight carry the agent away from the trap and it comes back to smell only once it is elsewhere. This is self-monitoring rather than per-lure boredom (#6), and it leaves norm

Area-restricted search. Food in this world is patchy — larder rooms hold two berries, trees two fruit, caves several mushrooms — so right after finding food the best place to look is nearby (including behind and beside, outside the 120-degree view), while in a barren stretch the best move is straight on. A PLENTY level rises when a seen morsel is within two cells of the agent, floods the map and fades over ~60 thoughts, and it weakens #7's ballistic muting of the frontier behind the agent: local, turning search just after food, long straight runs where there has been none. Base is #17 (frustration, body-honest diagonals, appetite, aversion, doors).

Corridor geometry, continuing the line that the field must respect the body (#15's honest diagonals were the last clear gain). A body of radius 0.45 threads a one-cell gap only after drifting onto its centre line and slides along both walls of a one-wide corridor, so such cells cost more time than open floor, yet the wave prices them alike. A cell walled on two opposite sides (a gap or corridor) now passes the wave at a small discount, so of two routes of nearly equal length the agent takes the wider one and loses less time wedged and centring; where a squeeze is the only way, the discount is small enough that the route still wins. Base is #17 (frustration + body-honest diagonals).

A test of what #8 really showed. The express wave lost 6.4 meals and killed 5 agents, and I blamed its speed; but its two-cell DIAGONAL hops were gated only by the middle cell, so they cut wall corners — exactly the fault whose repair in #15 was a gain. Here the wave gets two-cell hops only in straight lines through an open middle cell, discounted as two steps, so a new lure reaches the agent twice as fast and an eaten one's stale ridge fades twice as fast, while nothing passes a corner. If it wins, speed was never the problem and corner-cutting was; if it loses, the slow wave really is a sweet spot. Base is #17.

Confinement suppression divides EVERY lure by the solid around it, so a morsel the agent can actually SEE in a cave or a larder room — where much of this world's food is placed — is pulled at a fraction of its worth and loses to open frontier. The traps confinement was built against are uncertain lures (smell painted into a nook, frontier in a dead end). Here seen morsels pull at full learned appetite wherever they are, while smell (also muted by frustration) and frontier (also muted behind the agent) keep the confinement discount, so the agent goes into caves and rooms for food it has seen without being drawn into nooks by smell. Base is #17.

Unknown ground is a gamble the wave ignores. A cell nobody has seen passes value exactly like known floor, so a plan to a smell waypoint or a morsel glimpsed in clutter runs straight through fog that may hold a wall; the agent commits, meets the wall, and replans — and #21 just showed that targets in clutter really are worse than Bellman says (taking confinement off seen morsels cost 3.3 meals and two lives). Here every cell passes the wave in proportion to how sure the map is that it is walkable: known-free at full rate, unknown at a discount, so of two plans the one over ground already seen wins, and an approach through fog must be clearly shorter to be chosen. Base is #17.
